passage:
Day 4. Tejas woke at noon, the whole to-do list staring at him like a wall. That evening he told himself: if I can't do everything, I shouldn't try to do anything. Then he changed the thought. Just three things tomorrow. Up by eight. A real meal. Ten minutes outside.

Day 9. His roommate Tanuja saw him drinking tea on the balcony at eight-thirty and said nothing, only slid a plate of poha toward him. He whispered to himself, that's two.

Day 16. The list still had only three lines. But he also added a call with his mother, then a short walk to the tea stall. He noted that the small list didn't feel like giving up. It felt like holding on until his energy returned.

qa.q: What three tasks did Tejas set for himself?
qa.a: Up by eight, a real meal and ten minutes outside.

qa.q: What does Tejas's thought on Day 16 about the small list suggest about his feelings?
qa.a: Tejas feels a quiet steadiness and self-acceptance, seeing the short list as holding on rather than failing.

qa.q: What could Tejas do on a day when even three tasks feel too much, and why?
qa.a: Tejas could keep just one, such as a drink of water on the balcony, because a smaller step still keeps the habit and avoids the all-or-nothing trap.

qa.q: How might Tanuja see Tejas's change over those days?
qa.a: Tanuja may notice him surfacing slowly, with the plate of poha and the silence being a low-pressure way to show support.

grounding: On low days a person cuts demands to three basic tasks to save energy and gradually rebuilds from there.

subtype: Approach: cut all plans down to a minimum routine [Thinking]
passage:
Reena, you say even getting out of bed feels like climbing a hill some days. I believe you. Let your Bhupen mama tell you about a winter when I was twenty and felt the same.
I'd moved to Shillong for my first job, and somewhere in that cold, grey season everything went heavy. Every night I made lists: exercise, study for the bank exam, write home, clean the room. Each morning I did none of it, and felt worse for failing.
One Sunday I tore up the long list and asked myself: what is the smallest day I can still call a day? I wrote three things only. Get up at seven. Eat one proper meal, not tea and biscuits. Go outside for ten minutes, even just to the corner shop.
Some days that was all I did. But I did it, and it held me steady till spring. That spring I also went to a doctor, which I should have done sooner.
So, Reena. Three things. That's allowed.

qa.q: What were the three things on young Bhupen's short list?
qa.a: Get up at seven, eat one proper meal, go outside for ten minutes.

qa.q: How did young Bhupen feel after failing the long lists each morning?
qa.a: Worse and more discouraged, as each unfinished list felt like another failure.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Bhupen's story, and why did it help?
qa.a: Tearing up the long list for three small tasks; they were possible even on heavy days, so each day ended with something done.

qa.q: What would change if young Bhupen had kept the long lists?
qa.a: Each morning would likely have added another failure, deepening the heaviness instead of holding things steady.

grounding: Shows a person on low days cutting plans to three tasks: waking at a set time, eating properly and stepping outside briefly.

subtype: Approach: cut all plans down to a minimum routine [Thinking]
passage:
Semester exams started in nine days, the hostel internet had been down since Monday, and Sumit had spent three mornings in bed until noon, staring at a timetable that said 'revise four chapters a day'.
On Thursday his friend Hafsa, a senior who had once had a rough semester of her own, called from the next block. He admitted it: 'I can't do any of it. I just lie there.'
'Then don't do any of it,' she said. 'What's the least you can do and still call it a day?'
He thought aloud, slowly. 'Wake at eight. Eat breakfast in the mess, not just chai. Walk to the library and back, even if I don't open a book.' He paused. 'Three things.'
'Three things. Text me when each one's done.'
On Friday he did all three. At the library, since he was there anyway, he read ten pages. Saturday, three things again, and twenty pages. It wasn't four chapters. But it was more than zero, and he wasn't in bed at noon.

qa.q: How was Sumit feeling before Hafsa's call?
qa.a: Stuck and overwhelmed, lying in bed till noon, unable to face a plan that felt impossible.

qa.q: What else could Sumit add once the three things feel steady?
qa.a: Talking to a counsellor or teacher about the heavy days, and slowly adding a small study goal while keeping the three basics.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel getting Sumit's texts on Friday?
qa.a: Relieved and encouraged, seeing each small step done.

grounding: Shows a student on low days shrinking plans to three basics, waking at a set time, eating properly and going outside, to protect energy.
